dysmenorrhea-relief.question: What helps menstrual cramps, and does exercise make a difference?
dysmenorrhea-relief.summary: Over‑the‑counter medicines for menstrual cramps work well with very few risks [F1]. Heat therapy is likely to reduce menstrual pain intensity both during prophylaxis and acute episodes compared with no treatment [F3]. Heat therapy probably reduces the risk of adverse effects compared with NSAIDs, with a risk ratio of 0.30 [F4]. Heat therapy may provide comparable or slightly better pain relief than NSAIDs after three months, with a weighted mean difference of -1.10 cm [F6]. Regular exercise may reduce menstrual cramps [F2].

heavy-menstrual-bleeding.question: What are the treatment options for heavy menstrual bleeding?
heavy-menstrual-bleeding.summary: Pharmacologic treatments include tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraception, cyclical oral progestogens, and hormone therapy such as oral contraceptive pills, patches, or injections [F7][F4]. Gonadotrophin‑releasing hormone antagonists such as linzagolix and relugolix‑estradiol‑norethisterone acetate are recommended for moderate to severe symptoms of uterine fibroids [F2]. Hormonal intrauterine devices are inserted into the uterus to provide contraception and control bleeding [F6]. Endometrial ablation, including fluid‑filled thermal balloon and microwave techniques, is a surgical option when intervention is appropriate [F1][F3]. Hysterectomy, the removal of the uterus, is the most invasive surgical treatment [F8].

sub_answers.question: What pharmacologic therapies are effective for heavy menstrual bleeding?
sub_answers.answer: Tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraception, and cyclical oral progestogens are pharmacological treatments for heavy menstrual bleeding [F7]. Gonadotrophin‑releasing hormone antagonists such as linzagolix and relugolix‑estradiol‑norethisterone acetate are recommended as options in NICE technology appraisal guidance for treating moderate to severe symptoms of uterine fibroids in some people [F2]. Hormone therapy is commonly available as oral contraceptive pills, patches, or injections and is frequently prescribed by a health care provider before trying more invasive treatments such as endometrial ablation [F4]. Non‑hormonal medications like tranexamic acid and ibuprofen can be used to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding [F5]. Progestogen-only contraception may suppress menstruation and can be beneficial for women with heavy menstrual bleeding [F9].

sub_answers.question: What hormonal intrauterine devices are used to treat heavy menstrual bleeding?
sub_answers.answer: Hormonal intrauterine devices are inserted into the uterus to provide contraception and control bleeding [F6].

sub_answers.question: What surgical options are available for heavy menstrual bleeding?
sub_answers.answer: Endometrial ablation is a surgical option for heavy menstrual bleeding [F1]. Fluid‑filled thermal balloon and microwave endometrial ablation are recommended as options in NICE technology appraisal guidance when surgical intervention is appropriate [F3]. Hysterectomy, the removal of the uterus, is the most invasive surgical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding [F8].

hpv-cervical-screening.question: How does HPV relate to cervical cancer, and what screening is recommended?
hpv-cervical-screening.summary: Cervical cancer is caused by persistent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) [F1]. Persistent HPV infection of the cervix can lead to precancerous lesions which, if left untreated, cause about 95% of cervical cancers [F2]. Women should be screened for cervical cancer with a high‑performance test every 5–10 years starting at age 30 [F3]. Women living with HIV should be screened every 3–5 years, starting at age 25 [F4]. HPV nucleic acid testing, conventional cytology, and liquid‑based cytology each reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality [F9].

sub_answers.question: What is the role of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in the development of cervical cancer?
sub_answers.answer: Cervical cancer is caused by persistent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) [F1]. Persistent HPV infection of the cervix can lead to precancerous lesions which, if left untreated, cause about 95% of cervical cancers [F2]. Almost all cervical cancer cases (99%) are linked to infection with high‑risk HPV [F7]. Infection with a high‑risk HPV type is necessary but not sufficient on its own to cause cervical cancer, and most women with such infection do not develop cancer [F10]. Persistent HPV infection is the most important risk factor for developing cervical cancer [F11]. High‑risk HPV types are carcinogenic and are found in 99% of cervical precancers [F12].

sub_answers.question: What are the current evidence‑based guidelines for cervical cancer screening in women?
sub_answers.answer: Women should be screened for cervical cancer with a high‑performance test every 5–10 years starting at age 30 [F3]. Women living with HIV should be screened every 3–5 years, starting at age 25 [F4]. The global strategy encourages a minimum of two lifetime screens with a high‑performance test by age 35 and again by age 45 [F5]. Cervical screening from the age of 30 (25 years in women living with HIV) can detect cervical precancer, and when coupled with timely treatment can prevent progression to cervical cancer [F6]. 70% of women are screened using a high‑performance test by age 35 years and again by age 45 years [F8].
